utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. No preliminaries. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness, which will be Mr. Dodik, if I am well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, last warning, you'll be really removed from the courtroom if the same happens again. You remain seated, and there's no need to greet in the way you did. Apparently you think it to be funny, in view of your smiling. Last warning. Let that be clear. Good morning, Mr. Dodik, I presume. Mr. Dodik, before we start hearing your evidence, you are required to make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Dodik, I noticed already that you are a fast speaker. If you want your words to be interpreted in full, please slow down in your speed of speech. Mr. Dodik, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, President. I will be examining you now, and after your answers, I will make a short pause. It's not for you to add anything. It's for the interpreters to be able to finish. Would you please say, for the record, your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Milorad Dodik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Father's name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Bogoljub.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: 12 March, 1959 in Banja Luka. 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] In Banja Luka. [Interpretation] Could you say again the year when you were born and where.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: 12 March 1959, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What schools did you finish?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The faculty of political sciences in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just before the war, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I was president of the Executive Board for the municipality of Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember in which period?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The term of office was one year at the time. I was in that position in 1989/1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you run in the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For which party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I was on the ticket for the election unit of Banja Luka for the Alliance of Reform Forces of Yugoslavia. I was heading their ticket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the founder of that party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The founder was the federal prime minister, Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At those elections, were you elected to some position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Deputy to the assembly of what was then Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To conclude with your political career, after the war, did you continue in politics?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I founded a separate party, Independent Social Democrats; and in 1996, in the spring of 1996, while in 1998 in January, I was elected prime minister of Republika Srpska until January 2001. In 2006, in February, I was again elected prime minister, and at the elections that year, my mandate was renewed as prime minister. 2010, I was elected president of Republika Srpska. And in the October elections last year, I was re-elected for a new term. And I'm the president of the party which has the greatest support in all the elections in Republika Srpska since 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us cast our minds back to the political scene in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war in 1992. You said you ran in the elections for the reformist party of Ante Markovic and you were elected member of parliament. Of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. What was the leader of the party by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of that party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It reflected the structure of Yugoslavia. The party was first formed across the republics of Yugoslavia because there was no federal law on multi-party organising, and only when that law was passed just a few months before the elections, the party was established at the level of Yugoslavia. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the party was established and had its representatives in the Presidency and in lower units. All ethnicities of Yugoslavia were represented in the party, and our electoral ticket was multi-ethnic. I was president of that party for Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the platform of this multi-ethnic party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The key political issue at the time was how to preserve our common state of Yugoslavia, and representatives of that party wanted to come into positions in various republics and provinces to promote that issue and to prevent the breakup of the country, which actually happened just before the elections. Of course, free market, joining what was then the European community, democracy, multi-party system, a free market that were the main points in our programme. National equality and no discrimination on any grounds. I can go on, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I'm waiting for the interpretation. Did your party believe that some things have to remain joined in that state?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That it should remain a joint state, that was the commitment of everybody. At the time, we met members of our party from Slovenia and from Macedonia and everybody wanted to preserve Yugoslavia as it was, although reformed, and to promote the objectives that I just enumerated, and no republic or provincial organisation of our party had any other aims. Our first goal was to preserve the common state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before these multi-party elections, what was the political scene in Bosnia-Herzegovina like?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: One year before, the SDA, the nationalist party of the Muslims, was established, led by Alija Izetbegovic, a man who, for his promotion of Islamic radicalism had served a sentence in prison for promoting the idealogy of the Young Muslims, a man who authored the well-known book "The Islamic Declaration" where he listed his main beliefs and goals, that is to establish an Islamic order based on the sharia law and the idea that minorities should adjust to that order and that as soon as majority is achieved, the law of the sharia, in a way, it was a predecessor of the Islamic radicalism that we are seeing everywhere in the world now. He was surrounded by other members of the party who also had belonged before to the Young Muslims. During the Second World War, according to certain information, Alija Izetbegovic, who was born in Bosanski Samac, had been a member of the Handzar Division, a nationalist Ustasha organisation of that time. Later, a couple of weeks later, the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, was formed as the political organisation of the Croats, and that was a direct branch of the Croatian Democratic Union of Croatia founded by Franjo Tudjman, and only then was the Serbian Democratic Party formed, led by Radovan Karadzic, as a party uniting the Serbs. On the political arena there were several more parties, first of all, the Social Democratic Party, which was, in fact, a transformed League of Communists and the party I belonged to, the Alliance for Reform of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These five parties were the major political players during the elections, although there were younger parties as well, such as SPO, which had one seat in Parliament, a party that was promoted by the youth and also had one seat, a liberal organisation, a liberal party, however, the three political parties, the SDA, HDZ and SDS, got the majority vote each from their own ethnic community and took over power after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the relations between the ethnic parties before and after the elections?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: There was general tension immediately after the SDA was formed. They started a political drama. The HDZ was transferred to Bosnia, that and the forming of the SDS seemed to be a reaction to the founding of an ultra nationalist party among the Muslims which promoted the idea of pan-Islamic unity and radical Islam, as we may better understand it from the present time. There were individual incidents. The HDZ and the SDA promoted partnership before the elections and within their ethnic communities, the SDA, among the Muslims, and the HDZ, among the Croats, and the SDS, among the Serbs, got between 80 and 90 per cent of the votes from these ethnic groups. So very little votes remained for the other parties. As a political party, we had won a total of 12 per cent of votes in these elections. After the election, relatively quickly, for the political situation in the Balkans, in particular, when coalition agreements need to be harmonised, these three parties established joint power in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They've established the leadership in the Parliament and the then-Executive Council, which discharged the duties of the republican government. So there was a distribution of power within the coalition, depending on the number of votes they had won. These three political parties, I mean. It seemed that they were able to preserve peace. There were many Parliament sessions held and for more than a year, we were trying to resolve various issues within Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would like to say that already at that time immediately after the elections, the armed conflict had already broken out in Croatia. In June 1991, Croatia and Slovenia declared their independence that was supported by Germany, its foreign minister, Genscher, and after him, members of the European community, which were pressured by Germany to recognise these two republics so that the framework of the EU could be further developed. That's what we know now. In fact, that meant breaking up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the leading Bosnian politicians in terms of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and how was that reflected in the work of the Parliament?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The SDS policy was the -- for Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain in Yugoslavia. The HDZ, of course, as a party that was integrated with the Croatian HDZ, supported independence. The independence of Croatia, I mean. And that caused much turbulence within the Parliament and, of course, Party for Democratic Action led by Alija Izetbegovic, also supported the breakup of the country and the independence of Croatia and Slovenia. Under such conditions, it was very difficult to work. The party that I was a member of believed that the independence of Slovenia and Croatia ought not to be acknowledged and that Yugoslavia ought to be preserved. However, we were no longer a relevant political factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hold any talks or did you have any verbal duels with Alija Izetbegovic with regard to this issue?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Concerning the recognition of Croatia and Slovenia, Alija Izetbegovic abused the Parliament as a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina which had several members. I believe it was nine. He wasn't even the president of the Presidency -- or yes, he was. I'm sorry, he was at that particular moment. So he came to the roster -- to the rostrum in the Parliament and he said that he proposed for the Parliament to recognise Slovenia and Croatia as independent countries. I then asked him on what basis did he present that position. Was that the position of the then-Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or was it the position of his party and his own personal view? He said that it wasn't a harmonised position of the Presidency but that it was the position of his party and himself. I told him that he had abused the rostrum because no one entitled him to speak as an individual or the president of his own party and that he was not allowed to present views that had not been harmonised within the Presidency and it hadn't been harmonised. But such abuses were frequent. So it was no wonder that Alija Izetbegovic had abused the Parliamentary rostrum, to promote his own ideas in such a manner. And my duel with him ended there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did SDS view the secession of Croatia and Slovenia from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party was in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia and in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining within Yugoslavia. When it became obvious that that was practically impossible, then they insisted that the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina be recognised in terms of the status issues within Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. Let me just say that the then-constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina envisaged two-thirds majority for any change of status within the framework of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Socialist Republic, as it then was, protected the rights of the ethnic groups in a high degree. I have to say - and you all know - that according to the constitution of the then-Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the sovereignty was invested in the peoples, that is to say, the ethnic communities and the republics were political territorial organisational units of those peoples. Bosnia-Herzegovina had, within its composition, three main peoples or ethnic groups: The Serbs, the Bosniaks, or the Muslims as they were officially called at the time; and the Croats. And there were some nationalities or national minorities. They were called nationalities at the time. Now, we would call them national minorities. So in this regard, the SDS requested that the procedures provided by the constitution be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did these differences affect the co-operation between the ethnic parties that were in power at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It was already becoming difficult to hold Parliamentary sessions. One could see that other institutions of the executive powers had difficulties to function, but formally they were still in their place and functioning. It was obvious to see that the political representatives of the Croats and the Muslims co-operated and formed coalitions as to oppose any initiative coming from the Serbian side. They always refused such initiatives and there was a lot of animosity. The promotion of the independent Bosnia-Herzegovina was already underway and specific political moves were already being taken to that effect. An attempt to convene the Parliament on several occasions were unsuccessful because there were very long breaks and it was very difficult to finalise the sessions even if they began. The sessions used to last day in and day out at the time, so both during the day and then they would continue on into the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This discord among the political parties, how did that affect the three peoples living in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, the people were already homogenised around their political parties, that had happened before the elections already and as a rule, they followed their leaderships. And when the -- the armed conflict in Croatia is added as an additional factor, where the Serbs and the Croats were the main participants, then it's easy to imagine what sort of relations the Serbs and the Croats had between themselves within Bosnia-Herzegovina. The territory most populated by Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina borders directly Croatia, so most of the Serbian population from northern Bosnia were psychologically already involved in the conflict and they felt a solidarity with the Serbs in Croatia. Of course, on the basis of negative perception from the Second World War. Living along the Sava river during the Second World War, they were the victims of -- the then-independent state of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slow down. The interpreters have difficulties in following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You stopped where you said that during the Second World War ...

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. The Jasenovac camp. According to the information that I came across in several places and also at Yad Vashem centre in Jerusalem, the information is that 700.000 people were murdered, of which 500.000 were Serbs. Among the Serbs living in those areas, the memory of that suffering was very strong and affected their mentality and also was a cause of fear that something similar might happen again. And that was the atmosphere of the social and public life in the early 1990s. It is a fact that the Communist regime, because of its own ideological needs, had practically blocked the truth about Jasenovac to be published and the results were various speculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did all politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina observe the constitution and the concept of the constitutionality of peoples at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: According to the charter of the UN, the right of the people for self-determination belonged to the peoples rather than to the republics. That was how it was defined in the constitution of the SFRY at the time. The right to self-determination was not a matter to be decided by the republics but, rather by the peoples. It is easy to establish that; practically all republics were mono-ethnic. Slovenia comprised the Slovenes; Croatia, Croats as absolute majority; in Serbia, it was the Serbs; in Macedonia, the Macedonians, but in Bosnia-Herzegovina, matters stood differently. There were three constituent peoples; that is to say, the Serb, the Muslims and the Croats. According to the constitution of SFRY and the UN charter, they had the right to self-determination. The Serbs decided to remain within Yugoslavia; the Croats supported the independence of Croatia, believing that a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be joined to Croatia. And the Muslims wanted to impose their will both on the Serbs and the Croats and form an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did this principle of the constituency of the peoples mean in terms of the consensus of the three peoples? Where did this consensus have to exist? Could two peoples outvote the third in that sense? Can you just briefly tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The constituency meant that you were invested with sovereignty. According to the constitution of SFRY from 1974. Consensus was the only possible way to decide. It was the prescribed manner of taking decisions, up until the moment when the Party for Democratic Action, led by Alija Izetbegovic, and the Croatian Democratic Union had not decided to decide by a simple majority and end this whole story about constituency and consensus. Their policy was to abolish the constituency principle invested in the peoples because they had the absolute majority in the organs that made all the relevant decisions. But the majority was not qualified to make decisions. The majority had to include representatives of all three constituent peoples, but Alija Izetbegovic decided that that would no longer be so, and that, of course, caused a number of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the war, what was Alija Izetbegovic's attitude to this principle of the constituent status of peoples?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: He demolished that principle just before the war and that could have been the main reason for the war. Because if that principle had continued to be honoured, I'm convinced that the war wouldn't have happened. Political solutions would have been sought instead, as the Serbian Democratic Party wanted. I must say that I, myself, was never a member of the SDS. But Muslims and Croats at the time felt triumphant and ignored Serbian representatives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Alija Izetbegovic put a very dubious signature on the Dayton Accords, as the president of a Bosnia-Herzegovina that did not exist at all, nor was he its president. However, the countries that sponsored these accords believed that that's the way it should be. Even at the time Alija Izetbegovic continued to misrepresent himself, because he neither had Bosnia nor was he the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina when he put his signature on the Dayton Accords. Very soon after the Dayton Accords, which envisaged a Bosnia-Herzegovina as made up of two entities and three peoples, in its Article 3, one entity being a Federation of Muslims and Croats in the beginning, and, later it became the BH Federation, whereas, the other entity was mono-ethnic, Alija Izetbegovic decided to reform the Dayton Accords from inside. He asked the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down and repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're invited to slow down and to -- could you please resume from where you said: "Alija Izetbegovic decided to reform the Dayton Accords from inside," and could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what he decided. And he applied to the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the court to proclaim the constituent character of all the three people, Serb, Croats, and Muslims; that is to say, Bosniaks in the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The constitutional court did that when it was made up of nine judges, out of which six domestic judges and three foreign ones, whereas, four domestic judges were against and two Bosniak judges plus three foreigners, made this decision and proclaimed the constituent character of these peoples in the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the beginning of the erosion of the Dayton Accords and the disturbance of the balance established by those accords with the mechanisms of protection given to these peoples on a joint level and within the Federation. Alija Izetbegovic, when he had to abolish that constitutional character, did that and war ensued. And when he had to continue on the path of war by political means, he asked for and obtained the constitutional status for three peoples in the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the conviction that, in that way, he would achieve the domination of Bosniak Muslims in the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Today, as a result of that policy by Izetbegovic, we have across the board outvoting against the Croats in the Federation of Muslims and Croats, and the same thing is being imposed on the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, when you said "and war ensued," which war did you have on your mind? Because were talking about what happened after Dayton, and then war ensued. Which war did you have on your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is well known in theory and even in practice that the war objectives of Alija Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, if you just tell me what war you had in mind. You said "war ensued," and that was after --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Political war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Political war. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did the Serb politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina react to the erosion of this -- these constitutional principles?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: They demanded that these constitutional principles, the first of them being the constituent character of peoples, be honoured. But they were ignored. And the Serbs decided that within the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, among their own representatives, they should organise themselves in order to be able to carry on the political struggle against the political representatives of Muslims and Croats who were, by that time, united, allied. I believe everyone knows - and the Court knows - that until 1993, the ethnic group which, under the constitution of Yugoslavia, was called Muslims changed its name to Bosniaks, and that is the sense in which I use the term "Muslims" until 1993. So, the Serbs decided that their deputies to the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina should organise themselves into a deputies club of the Serbs and to try to ensure that the constitution continued to be honoured. I want to add that Communism recognised the fact that the constituent character of peoples is an important thing for peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this constituent status was abolished by Izetbegovic, not because he was promoting universal human rights and civil society, but because he was reckoning that he had the majority and that the Muslims, which in the last census before the war, made up 46 per cent of the population - that is to say, the majority - were able to impose their will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did the opposition parties view this idea of the cessation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: You mean parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Including your party.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The party that I belonged to split because the Muslim and Croat members of that party supported the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas, I personally did not support that policy. And the party disintegrated. As a rule, Bosniak members of that party continued to promote the policies of the SDA, the Croat members went on to support secession, whereas we Serbs continued to work for the preservation of Yugoslavia. SDP, formerly the Communist party, split in the same way, along ethnic lines, and there was practically no opposition from then on to ethnic rifts. Everybody believed, and I was a witness to that, that it was impossible to achieve consensus and respect for everyone and that under such extraordinary circumstances it was quite natural to promote the protection of the people that one belongs to, especially since I was able to see that others do not wish to respect others. They only want majority rule. Therefore, I had no hesitation in joining the Assembly of the Serbian People that was organised in November 1991 as a member of an opposition party, but I did not join the SDS. Throughout the war, I remained an independent MP and I was convinced that, in that way, I was meeting my obligation to the people I belonged to and that it was only fair. I still believe that today. Apart from very few people whose voices were not heard, everybody in all ethnic groups thought the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this trial, we heard a lot about the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What were the consequences of taking this decision on the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I must say that before that, on the 25th of January, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I meant the decision to organise the referendum in the October of the previous year.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: When the Serbian people turned out for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. I meant taking the decision to organise the referendum that would be held in February 1992, the declaration of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Oh, the declaration of the SDA. That complicated everything in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the maximum. But I believe in January 1992, the decision was taken to organise the referendum and that decision was taken without the participation of the Serbs. Not only the Serbs from the SDS, but without also the Serbs who were independent deputies. In November, when the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed, the main purpose of that assembly was to fight for equality in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was ignored, of course. And, thus, we reached the point of that illegal referendum because it did not respect the constitutional decisions on respect for all peoples. It was instead a manifestation of the political will and the arrogance of the Muslims and Croats. Today, when I speak to Croats from that time - and I know many of them - many of them say that, at that time, they were going to the referendum in the belief that it was a way of supporting the independence of Croatia; but in hindsight, today, they think they would never have turned out for the referendum otherwise. Because it was not only a referendum on the unilateral secession, but it was also the beginning of the majority rule of Muslims over Croats. That referendum was organised on the basis of an invalid decision of the Parliament at the time when the Badinter Commission had already been established to deal with the issues of Yugoslavia, and that commission pronounced that this decision on the referendum was not valid because it did not reflect the will of the people, and that's why Izetbegovic was forced to push on with the referendum and it was carried by the Muslims. The referendum took place on the last day of February and the first day of March. Only Croats and Muslims turned out. As far as I know, the turnout was 64 per cent, which is exactly the share of Muslims and Croats in the population, and the majority of them, of course, voted for the proclamation of independence. That decision did not take into account the constitutional principle that any change of status in the country must be supported by more than two-third majority, and the Croats and Muslims did not have a two-third majority that was necessary to proclaim an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask one more thing before the break. Under what conditions were the Muslim and Croat political leaders prepared to insist on the secession of Bosnia from the Federation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic stated in Parliament that he was prepared to sacrifice peace for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina and thus ushered the people into war. In other words, war could begin, because he called for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We'll continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Dodik. You may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back after 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are putting very broad questions to the witness which results in a mixture of facts and a lot of opinion as well. Could you please try to be as focussed as possible. We take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, Mr. Lukic, could you tell us whether we have a fully booked schedule this week? Because, if not, one would, I think, for next week we have only one witness scheduled. And could it be considered to add that witness to the -- to this week so that we could already start because that would accommodate very much one of us who has to do a lot of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will definitely check that, Your Honour. I cannot answer you with the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To push forward the witness who is scheduled for next week and see whether he can start or even complete his testimony this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hold on. I don't know which witness. I know one we cannot shift around at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know which one, but the one who is schedule at this moment for next week. I think it is Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That witness, I think you are talking about, is a protected witness and -- no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm thinking it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He is. If it's the first witness for the next week, it's protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he should be escorted by the lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second, please. One second, please. I have at this moment -- I have two witnesses for next week, one of them is Mr. Pavlovic, viva voce expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we do not have the decision for Mr. Pavlovic yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I know that. You get that very soon. If that assists you, we'll certainly accommodate you as quickly as we can. But, meanwhile, let's proceed with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Dodik. Mr. Dodik, apologies for dealing with administrative matters when you entered the courtroom. And, Mr. Lukic, please keep in mind what I said before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end of our previous session, Judge Orie observed that some of my questions were rather general. Let me ask you whether you are telling us what you told us from personal experience or was it somebody else who told you what was happening in the joint Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I was present there for days and nights practically on end, and I listened to people. I was a witness of talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in voting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, of course, whenever it was on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We mentioned the SDA memorandum. It is called, "The act on reconfirmation of the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's the official title, and the other one is the colloquial. The representatives of Croatian and Bosnian people withdrew from the federal organs of SFRY after that. It all took place on the 15th of October, 1991. How did that event, how did the 15th of October, 1991 affect you and your party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you remain in the Parliament, did you remain a member of your party? Can you explain the situation for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That was an act of unilateral secession that was unlawful, which did not observe the procedure that was envisaged for the changes of status in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unilateral secession is not envisaged by international law either. And the declaration itself was completely false. It requested the reconfirmation of the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia-Herzegovina was never a sovereign country, never in history, and the territory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... would you mind to focus on the question. Because this Chamber has heard a lot about what has happened on the 15th of October. So the facts are, to that extent, presented to us by both parties, and the question specifically focussed on did you remain a member of your party, did you explain -- whether you could explain that. So could you please focus your answer on that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, but I understood that the question was how I felt. In order to explain how I felt, I had to say what I previously stated. But specifically: Of course, it was contrary to my own views and it was contrary to what I knew about the procedures about legality and the legitimacy. I was disappointed, I was embarrassed and I previously explained that the party that I had been a member of had already ceased to exist. Its members including us, the deputies, could not get together and adopt our positions any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking with your colleagues of other ethnicities in the Parliament, the Croat, the Muslims, and the Serbs too, could you see whether they were aware of the dangers that might result from this issue of secession?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The Muslims were in euphoria. They believed that they were one step from forming a country in which they would be the dominant decision-making majority by abolishing the principles of constituency, they believed that together with the Croats this would have a sufficient majority to make decisions in Bosnia-Herzegovina as the majority. However, that was not sufficient. So the Bosniaks were convinced that they were doing a good thing, regardless of the fact that they outvoting others and violating procedures and doing that a continuous manner. The Croats, on the other hand, believed that Bosnia-Herzegovina was unimportant for them. It was important to legalize and accept the declaration and establishing of independent state of Croatia and most of them represented it like that. So joint actions with the Bosnians and making decisions jointly at the time, it was done only as a way of supporting the independence of Croatia rather than true support for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did the Serbs react after this, and after being systematically outvoted in the joint Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, of course, we continued with the attempts to work in the parliamentary bodies and the Parliament itself but that was very difficult and unsuccessful. I already said that, on 21st of November in 1991, practically all MPs or all MPs for the SDS and us who were already independent at the time got together in the Parliament building in Sarajevo and declared the founding of the Parliament of the Serbian people, or the Assembly of the Serbian People, meaning to formulate joint proposals that we would later present in talks with the Muslims and the Croats. That was all it was. Because the Muslims and the Croats had already been homogenised and this only seemed like a logical and legitimate step. Personally, regardless of the fact that I wasn't a member of the SDS then or ever after that, I believed that it was necessary for me to be there. Any policy outside the representation of my people was practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The SDA, except for being organised politically, was it organised in any other sense?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the key moments in the preparations for war. The so-called Patriotic League was formed. It was the military wing of the political party of democratic action that brought together the Bosniaks. In addition to the fact that, formally and legally, the Yugoslav People's Army was still the only legal army at the time, Bosnia-Herzegovina as a socialist republic had the right to organise its own Territorial Defence so it was the only entity that could do that. There was also the Ministry of Interior of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the police. In spite of all that, the SDA decided to form the Patriotic League, the armed wing of the party, whose role could be seen later in many of the events that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly tell us whether history had affected the way people think in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: History is being lived there. It was so at the time and it continues to be like that. The historical context, the historical developments in the area, affect the thought process of Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats as the dominant factor. It's a country in which consensus was ever hard to achieve. The three peoples were never on one and the same side in any important historical events. They were always on different positions as a rule, and antagonistic and inimical, not just in 1990s but throughout history. The fact that shows that best that, is for example, in Bosnia-Herzegovina even today or at the time either, it was not possible to harmonise anything. So that Bosnia-Herzegovina today has only two holidays that have been harmonised, the new year and Victory Day. Not a single historical event that would be celebrated jointly. If it is celebrated, then the peoples are on opposite sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me now return to the forming of the Assembly of the Serbian People. Before it was formed, did the Serb side attempt to make any agreements that was mentioned, but can you tell us anything specifically about such attempts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It's a fact that the Executive Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time still had the Serbian representatives. They were not withdrawn and it tells you all. Momcilo Krajisnik as the Parliament Speaker regularly convened Parliament sessions in an attempt to observe the procedures and to -- have the issues resolved by putting them on the agenda of the Parliament. I know that there were attempts to hold talks between Karadzic and Izetbegovic. At the time, I think that Kljuic was the president of the HDZ. We waited long for them in the various rooms in the Parliament, waiting to see if they would reach an agreement. So I used to sit there with others waiting for them to come out with some proposals. What I could hear was that the Serbs proposed the mechanism of protection of peoples when making decisions. They requested that there should be no outvoting when major issues were discussed but that was, of course, refused as we know today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina begin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I already said --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I mean the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In the neighbouring Croatia, which was still one and the same country, certainly mentally and also formally, that was where the armed conflict started, but the first casualties fell far from the areas where Serbs were dominant in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was in the Krajina, the Bosnian Krajina as it was called at the time, and there were also victims in Sarajevo, when at a Serbian wedding the bridegroom's father was killed which upset the entire Serbian community at the time. But it was considered to be a terrorist act, something that was unacceptable as it was a wedding, and that for ethnic reason, hatred of the Serbs, someone believed himself motivated enough to kill the bridegroom's father who was a member of the wedding party. Of course, after that, the activities of the previously mentioned Patriotic League took place in Bosanski Brod area and in some other places, practically as a series of events. Perhaps I should draw everyone's attention to another thing. Then, in those first months, the death of one person was a very disturbing fact. Unfortunately, later during the war, numbers of victims would cause less media attention than this one single death caused at the beginning of the war. So, of course, then the conflicts followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Bosanski Brod. Did Bosnian politicians go to the place of that incident in the village of Sijekovac in the municipality of Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, some of the politicians were there. I think Fikret Abdic was there; Biljana Plavsic was there. What we knew then, and it was noted at the time, that the victims were civilians. However, the events that were catching up overshadowed that visually and mentally so the incident was never investigated sufficiently. Only after the war was that matter looked into further but it was known that the Patriotic League committed crimes against the Serbian civilians in that village, and that was not something that was disputed by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Immediately before the war, before the conflicts broke out, did you attend meetings where key political topics were discussed as well as the strategy of the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I've already stated that I was a member of the Assembly of the Serbian People which was later the Assembly of Republika Srpska, the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. I did take part in most of the meetings whenever I was able to attend them then and, of course, later during the war as well. I know that the assembly was adopting all the important constitutive laws for the establishment of Republika Srpska. I voted in favour of many of those documents. I considered them to be legal and legitimate. As I said, the SFRY constitution envisaged that the sovereignty should rest with the peoples, that the Serbian people had the right to their sovereignty and to their own decisions. So practically in all the constituent documents, I was present when they were being adopted. This was on the 21st of November and then later at an assembly sessions that were held in Sarajevo and then later in Pale. All the assembly sessions during the war. It's possible that I was absent from some of them due to combat, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the assembly session at which the six strategic goals were discussed of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That topic about the goals was something that appeared for a while, and it required the input of people from out in the field. It required definitions, setting up a certain framework relating to the political goals of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course, the basis of that was the strengthening of the constitutive aspect of the actual republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Taking part in these numerous assembly sessions and other kinds of meetings, did you ever see any kind of plan, oral or written, for Muslims and Croats to be expelled from territories under Serbian control?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't even a goal. Not even an unwritten one. Actually, there were attempts in the National Assembly of Republika Srpska to include representatives of Bosnians from the territory of Krajina who were there. I took part in conversation with one of those Bosniaks who agreed to something like that, but probably later, because of combat, he did not appear again. He left that area. The term "ethnic cleansing" is something that I heard only later, primarily from the media. It was something that appeared in the media while reporting on the situation from the region. The policy at the time was not a policy of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any discussions at the assembly that would encourage warmongering?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Were deputies who were casualties already at the beginning of the war. There was a Serb deputy who was killed on his way back from an assembly session while the joint assembly session was still working. It was the deputy from Srebrenica, Zekic, he was killed. Of course, that gave rise to emotions and in the throe of emotions it was very difficult to control the situation. However, we took into account decisions. That was important. Not just the discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a little bit earlier that you spoke with a representative of the Muslim people. Do you remember what his name was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mevludin Sejmenovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Ah, yes, yes. He was from Kozarac. He had relatives in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly tell us what that conversation was like, what that meeting was like?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: He had relatives in Banja Luka, so he was in Banja Luka. Deputy Vojo Kupresanin asked me if I would go with him and speak with this man and include him in our work. So I went to that house in the outskirts of Banja Luka in the Vrbanja settlement and we talked with him. Of course, at the time he was not quite clear on everything but he did not reject outright the possibility of becoming a member of the assembly with the other ethnic groups and to fight to preserve the peace which, at the time was still possible. I didn't see him after that, however, and I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will finish a little bit earlier. I just wanted to give a heads up to my colleague so he could get ready for his cross-examination. Talking about the six strategic goals of the Serbian people. One of those goals was the separation from the other two ethnic groups. How did you understand that and how was this discussed at the assembly? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims had already separated politically and institutionally. It had already happened. So it was just a matter of legalising the existing situation. So I understood that as an institutional political establishment and affirmation of national interests. It was never stated outright nor is it stated in any document that the Serbian people did not wish to agree and have a consensus with the other two peoples. So I know what the discussions are about that and all the back and forth. So as somebody who was politically engaged at the time I would not wish to be part of a structure that was in favour of divisions on the basis of ethnic cleansing, killings and so on. That was not the intention. I'm not saying that perhaps in view of some events that occurred later they did not contain some elements of that. However, but there was no evidence that the political decisions at that time were motivated by the -- the desire for physical divisions. We could explain it most easily by saying that, to date, we had all lived together and from now we would life side by side with each other, and that was how I viewed that in the political sense, not in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: President Dodik, thank you very much. These are all the questions that the Defence of General Mladic had for you. And thank you very much for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, in your 65 ter summary other subjects are mentioned but you leave them out, such as -- okay. Then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you want explanation I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's up to you. But I take it that if you tell us in advance what is there to be expected, that if it's different that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first conversation actually I had with Mr. Dodik last night and he had a severe migraine so I covered only topics he was able to discuss and I tried to cut this examination as short as possible to spare him from further suffering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Dodik, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger. You find Mr. Tieger to your right. Mr. Tieger is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, President Dodik.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Good morning to you as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by focussing, at least the initial part of the examination, on information you have been able to provide the Court previously. And just to clarify it's correct that you testified in the Brdjanin case at the end of July, beginning of August 2003; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. We were there together, you and I. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, not -- I think not in the Brdjanin case, Mr. Dodik. But we were there together when you testified in the Karadzic case in 2013. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: But if I may explain. I think that before I testified in the Brdjanin case, you and I had several meetings, I think. I think that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Dodik. And in addition to the meetings that you and I had, just a couple of weeks before the Brdjanin testimony, you also gave an interview to OTP representatives about the upcoming Brdjanin issues and that interview was tape-recorded. That's also correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, probably it was. You were recording it. I -- I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think we may have occasion to refer to that. I can show you the beginning of that interview and who was present at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I mentioned, I wanted to -- in the interests of efficiency, ask you whether you stood by some of those -- some of that information you provided previously. Again, I appreciate that in the Karadzic case, you indicated that whatever you said in the Brdjanin case and whatever was recorded you would stand by. But the nature of our process is such that I will be asking you about the specific portions and asking you to confirm those. So it may seem a little tedious but that's the nature of the process. So, first, I'd like to ask you -- you -- you provided information today -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: May I? I am going to tell you again that I stand by what I officially said before this Tribunal in the Karadzic and the Brdjanin case and what I was telling you in informal meetings was perhaps part of an impression or something, but in any case, I can always stand behind my publicly expressed positions here before this Tribunal. So I can understand your attempt now to look for inconsistencies, but I would not wish to change anything I said in the Plavsic case, in the Brdjanin case, and in the Karadzic case. I would not wish to change any word, line, sentence. I stand by all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Earlier today you were asked about the three national parties. You provided some focussed information about what you considered to be aspects of the SDA, and were relatively brief about the SDS, so I wanted to ask you more about the SDS, particularly in light of what you said before. So when you testified in the Brdjanin case, and I'm going to call up the particular transcripts so the parties and the Court can see it and well. That's 65 ter 33545. And that was on the first day of your testimony. E-court page 25, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: If I may assist, it's all right. What I said. It's okay. I -- I don't know what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let Mr. Tieger just ask his questions and there's no need also for us to understand what you are still standing by. We would have to know what it was. So, therefore, wait for Mr. Tieger's questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I appreciate the effort at moving us along. You were asked at transcript page 20468 of that case: "Was the party controlled from the top?" Referring to the SDS and you answered: "Yes, absolutely. Mr. Karadzic was the president of that party, which had its Main Board." And later in that -- on that same page, you were asked and then continuing, I think -- yeah, later on the same page: "Now, if the Main Board issued instructions, were the Municipal Boards and regional boards obliged to carry out those instructions?" And you answered: "Yes, that was quite clear. This was a firmly organised political party with clear-cut hierarchy and superior -- superiority." So I just want to ask if you stand by that particular portion of what you said in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course, I do. And it's absolutely correct. Just as it applied to all the political parties at that time, there was a hierarchical structure, a common policy, the president, the Main Board, which runs that party. I said that I wasn't a member of it but it was evident that the Municipal Boards and the lower-ranking organisational units, those forms of organisation, were in keeping with the policy that prevailed at the time. And this was something that was confirmed by the Main Board of that party. Is it possible for me to have the transcript in Serbian before me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Dodik, we don't have Serbian translations of the document which is why I'm reading very slowly and also ensuring that Mr. Lukic is aware of what page I'm referring to so he can follow it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue dealing with all the testimony, Mr. Lukic, I saw in the Defence exhibit list, reference to testimony in the Karadzic case 2nd of February, 2011. Whereas I'm now hearing that it was 2013. And any explanation for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says on the document it's 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I have got a copy which says 2011, but perhaps -- and that says Defence exhibits for Witness Dodik, Milorad, viva voce. That gives one exhibit number; that's "The Islamic Declaration" and then prior testimony, one, two, three and there it says 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's our mistake, our typo. But I don't think that the Prosecution had a problem with locating the previous testimony of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wondering whether I'm missing something and so where you earlier said it says 2013, you say it may be a mistake that the document says 2011.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No the document says '13, the transcript. The transcript says '13. It's typo on our information report on our table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So the information report is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning to the next page, e-court page 26, you were asked how strong was the control and discipline that was exercised by the SDS over these bodies where they were the controlling party. And you answered: "I think that this party was internally highly homogenised and it functioned in a highly disciplined fashion." And you confirm that today as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course, I think it should be noted that I said I think; I wasn't in the party. Of course, this also applied to the HDZ and the SDA. They were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the next page, e-court page 27, you were asked what happened to members of the SDS who didn't agree with some of the decisions that were made. And you responded: "Well, I think that they were minimised then, and that they turned passive." I take it you confirm that as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That happens still today. In my own party. I do confirm it. Yes, of course, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At page 50 of the e-court, and that's transcript page 20493, continuing onto your testimony on July 31st, 2003, you were asked: "So as far as the authorities in Banja Luka during this period May of 1992 until around September, the decision-making was that being made by the SDS? Is that what you're saying?" And you answered: "Well, the SDS was the party in power, and at that time it certainly conceived of the policy that was pursued at the time by the organs that functioned as state organs." And I presume you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That is very logical. My party today also sets policy and does that in the government, so that's how it was there too. I -- I confirm what is there, and I'm just adding what I have said now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it would be very helpful for everybody in the courtroom, especially for the interpreters and transcriber, to indicate from which line you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn back to page 26 of the e-court. That's 20469 and on this occasion lines 9 through 15. The question was asked: "Now, we've spoken about the community of municipalities and then the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the Assembly. You were not a member of the assembly, I think you've already told us. What sort of authority did that regional assembly have in respect of the municipal assemblies of the various municipalities that made up the autonomous region." And you answered the: "The assembly and the executive organ that was formed later, regulated all of life, political, economic, cultural, all segments of life. Decisions were passed and these decisions were observed by the municipalities that were members of these regional committees [sic]."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Communities. Excuse me, misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it you confirm that, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. May I just ask something about this? What is the document that you are presenting to me? It's my -- was that my testimony in the Brdjanin case or is that my conversation or my interview with you before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, so you won't -- there's no risk of confusion, Mr. Dodik, I'm talking it one step at a time. This is the transcript of your testimony from the first day in the -- you testified in the Brdjanin case. When I move to the second day, I will move you. And when I move to the tape-recorded interview, I will also advise you explicitly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we turn to page 47 of the e-court which would be 20490 in the paginated version. Lines 13 through 17. You were asked: "Now you've told us that the regional assembly because of the hierarchies established within the SDS had power over the municipal assemblies. Did the regional Crisis Staff, when it was set up, have the same powers as the assembly?" And you answered: "I think so." You confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think so, yes. But I did not have sufficient insight into all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning to e-court page 77, transcript page 20520, lines 13 through 19, no excuse me. Let me -- turn to e-court page... 78. At line -- transcript page 20521, and beginning at lines 3, you were asked: "How about a gentleman named Ljuban Ecim? How powerful was he?" You answered: "I think that he was a highly positioned member of the state security ... in Banja Luka, in that region. I think that he was deputy chief of that service." Question again was: "You mentioned in some conversations that you had with another Prosecutor, Mr. Tieger, that you saw him as being Karadzic's protege, a person who was close to Arkan, and you said that nothing could be done in Banja Luka without passing it through state security, through him. Do you still believe that to be the case?" And you answered: "In a certain period of time, yes." The question was asked --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It's common knowledge that Mr. Ecim was in the state security and that this State Security Department was under the influence of the state authorities. That's quite logical. As for the rest, it's a matter of perception that can be accurate or not. In any case, at the time, that's what it appeared to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the conversation -- the -- the questioning on the subject continues. So you were asked: "You said, this on page 3 of those notes: The fame and notoriety called of Ljuban's group was very strong everywhere in Banja Luka and everyone lived in fear of that group. He was, on the one hand, Karadzic's protege in Banja Luka, and on the other hand, he was very close to Arkan and his people. He managed to create the impression that he was Karadzic's person there and that he was untouchable." And you answered: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I have already said that was my perception, that's what it looked like. Whether it was accurate, time has shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 84 of the e-court, transcript page 20527.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek clarification of the last answer. You said whether it was accurate, time has shown. Now, that's ambiguous because time could have shown that it was or that it was not accurate. Did you intend to say that time has shown that it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that that was the general perception. And to the question whether he was close to Karadzic and Arkan, I said yes. In the time since then, I believe various studies have shown that. I did not express any views of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see that. But when you said time has shown, you were referring to studies which confirm what your impression was at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know whether it was confirmed or proven wrong. I didn't go into that, but the perception was as reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm informed that if you move to page 84 in - I take it that's the e-court page - there's private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. And it was based on Mr. Dodik's request at the time and the Karadzic case this very same issue was raised and Mr. Dodik indicated he didn't consider that necessary so this discussion took place in public and I -- I assumed that for essentially if they could be considered protective measures previously they had been varied by the Karadzic Chamber in light of the witness's request. We can redact it and move into private session if you think that's best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- I'm just informed. Was it officially, was the confidentiality officially lifted or do you just say that the way in which they dealt with it in the Karadzic case shows that confidentiality was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can read the precise line to you and maybe better to go into private session for the moment and I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we want to be rather precise on the procedural aspects of lifting confidentiality. We move into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Mr. ... what's -- Mr. Lukic, could you check with Mr. Mladic what is of his concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The break is here so I will check it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00, but not until after the witness has followed the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, we'll continue. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Karadzic, Krajisnik, Stanisic, Mandic, Zupljanin and Ecim were part of one small compact team and they were the most powerful people on their respective levels at the time. Even later, regardless of where they went, they still cling together. Can you confirm the accuracy of that, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, their appointments to various positions at that time enabled them to be in power. Just as I now today have the powers of the president of the republic, they had certain powers at that time, and they were in a position to co-operate with each other. So they had these formal positions. They got a lot of media coverage, regardless of the situation. The security situation was grave at the time, and, of course, people wanted the opinion of the minister of the interior. How else? You can also interpret it in the way you did, in the way you formulated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. May I -- I'm going to this at that case I think is best to tender the excerpt from case previously identified, in the transcript reference previously identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only this page, then. Mr. Lukic, any problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And earlier I think the -- we heard the witness say something about the accuracy of what he testified about before in this Tribunal. You have not uploaded that one page. Then, Mr. Registrar, could we reserve a number for the one page still to be uploaded and to be -- sought to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P7756, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that number is reserved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, I'm going to move on to the second day of your testimony in the Brdjanin case. That was August 1st, 2003. That is reflected at 65 ter 33546, and I'd like to turn, first, to e-court page 9 which is transcript 20542, lines 2 through 9. And you were asked: "You talked yesterday in response to some questions from Ms. Korner about discipline within the ranks of the SDS, and you told us that someone who openly disagreed with SDS policy would be punished and termed a traitor and disciplined in some way. Can you name anyone and specifically from the Krajina area, who was disciplined because of their disagreement with SDS policy? " And you answered: "In those days, or generally speaking for the whole period?" And the response came back: "In those days, I'm talking about translate 1991 and through the fall of 1992." And you answered: "I can confirm that the SDS was a compact, well-structured organisation in which the hierarchy was respected. And I do know that differing views, even though they wanted to present themselves as a democratic party, were not really tolerated, especially not at that time. And still less was their tolerance for behaviour that could be interpreted as not being in conformity with the policy of the party. I can't remember a single name, but there were many people in the past who were in the SDS and because they acted differently, they left the party. I think that Mr. Brdjanin himself left the SDS later on." And can you confirm that transcript reference, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Even now in my party I have many people from the former SDS. What am I supposed to confirm? What I said or can I comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... accuracy of what you said. I'm not looking for an expansion, in particular, and so I'm not inviting it, but if you feel one is necessary for some reason, I'm not precluding it. So essentially as I indicated before, I just am asking you to whether you stand by that testimony in the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it, and I've said before I stand by everything I've ever said before this court. Perhaps there's one thing that should be added. At least it seems to me now that the question was formulated in such a way as to require someone to say that somebody had a -- ruled the SDS with an iron hand. I had not noticed that before, but now I would like to say this. The SDS was a voluntary organisation, and there was self-discipline at lower levels and the higher level was respected in its decisions. It was rather compact, but nobody was physically forced to comply. There was no repression. There was just acceptance of that policy. So, if somebody later on came into conflict, they would either leave the party or would be disciplined by the party, according to their rules. I don't see any problem with that because that's the way it still functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to move next to e-court page 10 and 11 from the same day of testimony. And at transcript page 20543, you were asked to look at an interview dated 27 February 1992. That's found at about lines 9 and 10 of that page. An interview conducted of Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Krajisnik. Then you were asked: "Krajisnik at the time was probably one of the top three most powerful people in the SDS. Would you agree with that?" Your answer was: "Yes. He was a strong man of the SDS." And then moving on to -- you were then asked if there was a disagreement or if that interview reflected a disagreement between Brdjanin and Krajina about two or three matters. You said: "Yes, it's visible their views differed." Then asked: "Was Brdjanin, in effect, in this public interview diverging from the SDS line and the SDS policy?" You said: "Yes, that can be seen in the positions that are reviewed here." And then on the next page you stated: "Later on, Karadzic came to Banja Luka to discipline the Banja Luka organisation, and after that, the organisation came under the direct control of the top leadership in Pale." And do you stand by that testimony, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't see any difference with what I've said here earlier today. But in any case, it is quite customary for political parties at lower levels to have to comply with decisions of the higher level, and when there is a problem or a conflict, higher level has to deal with it. I think that it is quite proper and I have no proper in confirming that such things happened. I will say again I was not a member of the SDS, and I could only draw inferences based on things I saw or the perception that was created at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, just to be fair, those inferences that you drew and explained in the Brdjanin case were based on not only what you saw, but discussions you had with members of various parties at various times, including those which confirmed your impressions; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: A lot of time has passed, but I confirm what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next to the interview, the tape-recorded interview, you gave to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor a couple of weeks before you testified in the Brdjanin case. That's 65 ter 24921 -- 33531, excuse me. An interview conducted in Banja Luka on the 17th of July, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Did I know that it was being tape-recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, let's turn to the -- and the -- let's turn to the first page of that interview. In both Serbian and English. Mr. Grady introduces himself as an investigator working for the ICTY and for the Office of the Prosecutor. He identifies the certified interpreter with him and the very first thing he asks is: "Now, Mr. Dodik, are you aware that this conversation is being tape-recorded. Your response is: "Yes, I am." And Mr. Grady asks then: "And we have your permission?" And you respond: "Yes, you do." I'd like to turn then to page 3 of the interview in English and page 3 in Serbian.
