Mr. Grady asks you: "What do you feel was the purpose of this community of Bosanska Krajina municipalities? Why put these municipalities together." And you responded: "The SDS that presented itself at the time as the protector of the Serbian people publicly said and spoke that the Serbian people had to be protected from the Ustasha and other massacres as they used to say. Very often, they would go back to the stories from the Second World War, although factually, and in, in essence, the idea was to gain power and to gain control over the whole area and to rule through the social institutions." Do you stand by that answer given on July 17th, 2003, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't confirm anything that I've said to you outside of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I would tender this excerpt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P7757, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. How many pages is it, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is one page, Mr. President. I'll have a few more -- potentially a few more excerpts from the same interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would that all then be separate exhibits or would you join --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think they can be joined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you later indicate what pages they are and I take it this one-page upload will then be replaced by a multi-page upload.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That sounds more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, perhaps needless to say, the fact that you say I don't confirm anything doesn't change the evidence, that that is what you have said at the time and is recorded. Therefore, if you say that's not what I said, I contest that the recording is accurate, we'd like to know so that we can verify that, listen to the recording and ask for confirmation of the accuracy both of the recording and the translation. If, however, you say, Well, I don't want to confirm it, then, of course, the Chamber may consider what the reason is that you, as a general statement say, I'm not going to confirm anything which I didn't say in court, because why not? Is there any reason? If you have changed your mind since then, please let us know. Perhaps also explain to us why you have changed your mind. Because then we can include that in our considerations. If, however, you say, Whatever I said out of court, I -- I'm not willing to confirm that without any further explanation, of course, we'll then consider that situation. The text is, however, then admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I'd like to turn --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, well, if I may just -- and thank you for your clarification. I could talk based on my perception and, of course, my perception then and now is different. I think it would be good and I'm reading what's recorded here, I don't see any problems in the statement itself, especially as it's evident later that I said quite clearly that I was not a member of this assembly, so I was able to comment on it as someone who was an outsider. And earlier at the beginning of my testimony I also talked about my perception in view of the massacres of the Ustashas against the Serbs during the World War II, that this was something present in the people's emotions. So it's not a problem for me to confirm it, but I have to tell that you the definite reason is that I used to trust earlier what the Prosecution did and I trusted them more before than I do today. So that's probably the reason. I'm not so certain of the objectivity of everything that the Prosecution is doing. So though I respect you, having this in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... first of all, I thought it was fair to inform you about the legal situation. Second, if you say, I don't trust the Prosecution as I did before, then, of course, what we primarily look at is at your answers so as long as you trust yourself, that, I think, may be more important because it's -- it's the statement you gave. But if you say, well, some matters I could confirm; others may be a perception which has changed, then, of course, perhaps sometimes you wouldn't know exactly on what a perception at that time was base, what new facts there are now available to you which may change your perception of the situation. So therefore, I leave it to some extent to yourself, but since you gave a rather sweeping statement that you're not going to confirm anything that you didn't say in court, that's the reason why I raised the matter. Let's move on and you now know what your options are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to turn next to pages 4 and 5 of the English and page 5 of the Serbian. You were asked: "Do you recall speeches that he made within the assembly when you were a delegate with him." You asked: "You mean Brdjanin?" Answer was: "Yes." You said: "He said what the majority of the people from the SDS used to say at the time and he was active in many" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Public debates."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in English we're moving to -- about to move to the next page. This is at the very bottom. "And I think with hindsight, I think that he was more active verbally than actively participating in many things. There were many discussions at the time about the preservations, which the SDS advocated that Yugoslavia should be preserved. And I can tell you I think that his nature, his personality, made him participate a great deal in that. I can't remember specific things but --" And then you were asked: "What do you mean by his nature and personality?" And you answered: "How shall I explain. He was ... he was very exposed when it came to expressing certain standpoints but if you would like me to give you a psychological opinion, he was some form of a choleric temper. And people like that were used very well by the SDS at the local level. And when I look now it seems to me, seems to me that there was a group of people that the SDS used to use and when I say the SDS, I mean the leadership from Pale. And there was another line which was in charge of the party obedience and they were in charge of things that were happening in the field." Do you stand by those answers given in July 2003, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: As I have occasion to say that I have no problem with myself or my previous statements. I see no purpose in this reading out. I can confirm this if that's what you need and I think this does reflect my views at the time and how I saw those matters. But without intending to show a lack of respect to anyone, I think that what I say should also be respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dodik, you are here -- you're called by a party. You have to answer questions. That's simply so. If -- if you say I'd rather not answer some questions, that's not what this Court will respect because you are under a duty to do so. You have now said that that is how you perceived the matter at the time, certainly when you gave the statement. Is your nowadays-perception different from then? And if so, tell us in what respect it is different, and also tell us what made you change your perception. So let's take it one by one. Is your nowadays-perception different from the previous one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these statements, I don't have specific different perception but I'm just saying that time is also a factor in all of this. And as for the statements given outside the Tribunal and the courtroom, let me just tell you one thing. In my political career, I have given around 6.000 various political statements. I remember some of them; others, I don't know. Some were politically motivated, which was quite logical because that -- politics is what I do. So with regard to the statements given here at the Tribunal, I stand by all the transcripts and everything that was said. As for something that I said outside of the courtroom, there may be differences because I have not authorised the form of this statement. This is the first time I see it. Or at least I don't remember that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, let's try to get things straight. First of all, you said your perception is not different now but you say time plays a role. Then, that's still a bit ambiguous because if it's the same then apparently time in this respect has not played a role. But if you think that there are any difference over time that you changed your perception, please tell us and we'll consider that. Second, I hope that when you're interviewed as a witness or a potential witness, that if you compare that with political statements that you have stuck as much to the facts as any political person would do if he is interviewed as a witness and not as a politician. I leave it to that. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next to page 6 of the English and 6 of the Serbian. And in the Serbian, it's toward the bottom of the page. And in the English, it's in the middle, beginning around line 14 or so. You were asked -- still talking about Brdjanin in that context, of course. You state -- you then refer to a very -- well, I'll read the start: "Formally Brdjanin was the president, but as I said before, I think there were people in this Crisis Staff that far more powerful than him and all the decisions that were brought there were basically, prior to that, discussed and agreed to in the SDS. Because they had established a very strict party, as you say, discipline and whoever - even once - didn't fit into one of their arrangements, he was eliminated permanently." And then you were asked: "That was my question. How, how members were chosen for this very important body, this ARK Crisis Staff which certainly had influence on all the other municipal Crisis Staffs, how did they, how did they choose these members?" And you answered: "As I said before, it was arranged prior to anything in the SDS, the party that was in power at the time, and then they would appoint the people into the Crisis Staff. Because in, within their party structures, they decided which people those were ..." Okay. And I think... okay. Then there's a cough. Someone says excuse me, and then you continue: "... and simply, the -- those people were then just appointed later on" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please move to the next page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "And sometimes those people were those who they really didn't want to be there and didn't even belong to that party. But to refuse participation in this, for some people it was the same thing as execution. Nobody offered me though." Then you were asked: "Okay, could Brdjanin --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Could Brdjanin have become president of the ARK Crisis Staff without the blessing or, or authorisation of Radovan Karadzic? " And you answered: "I don't think so." And then moving a couple of lines down, you were asked: "And these other members of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Vukic, president of the SDS in Banja Luka." And you answered: "Yes, he was the president of the SDS. I think that, as the practical side was concerned, he was the most important person in all of this. He had to have full support and absolute support of the, approval of Karadzic, because without it he couldn't have been the president, which also gave him power at the local level." And then you were asked: "And are you aware of the, of the co-ordination that -- that took place between the ARK Crisis Staff and the various municipal Crisis Staffs within the region?" And you answered: "I think that they functioned jointly and that the orders that the regional Crisis Staff gave to the local Crisis Staffs were respected." Now, Mr. Dodik, do you stand by those answers in July 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Just add at the beginning what you skipped deliberately and that was that I was not a member and that I was able to say this based on my conversation with certain people. As for everything else, I agree. But you intentionally skipped that on the previous page. Before you started reading out all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a kind of accusation. You may answer the question. Whether Mr. Tieger did that deliberately or not, we'll consider that. If you say you left out this and this and that's important, you have an opportunity to do so. But we're not here in a courtroom to say that someone is trying to mislead you or mislead this Court because Mr. Tieger, first of all, we have the page there, we'll read the whole of the page if it's in evidence so, therefore, there's no need to make these kind of observations. Please refrain from it. These two pages which are pages 6 and 7 in the hard copy will be added to the excerpt that will be later uploaded under the number reserved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can we turn to page 15 in the English and page 17 -- 16, excuse me, in the Serbian. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There, Mr. Dodik, you were asked: "Can you give me other, any other sense of the, of the real hierarchy that went on within the SDS?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to move to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where are we on the B/C/S page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We should be where it begins [B/C/S spoken] it's -- the problem I have, there's a different pagination in this printed version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the bottom like the bottom third, bottom second third of the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, I think you found that, where it begins [B/C/S spoken] and I believe the Court has it now. "Can you give me any other sense of the -- of the real hierarchy that went on within the SDS and how it controlled these regions and then the locally municipalities?" And you answered: "Well, it's quite clear. They had their own people in the municipalities, that is the Municipal Board ... presidents of the Municipal Boards and the leadership of these boards and they were elected with full approval of Karadzic and the leadership from Pale, otherwise, they couldn't have been elected. Then, a very important part was played by the delegates from that area, from his party ..." And then after going briefly off tape because someone is sneezing. Turn the page, please, in Serbian, you continue: "Then there was their people who were posted in the media, in the police and other structures and at one point, the commissioners of the SDS Main Board, of the top of the SDS, were appointed, so these are the people from the core leadership, who were placed in charge of a certain region." Mr. Dodik, do you stand by those answers again in July of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That was the factual situation. If I may add, today you cannot elect a representative of a local organisation without the approval of the president of the party. That's the situation today in the Balkans even today and even in my own party the one of which I am the president. So that was just normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender that excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would then be at least English text on pages 15 and 16. And the corresponding B/C/S pages, Mr. Tieger, I take it that you'll carefully select them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They will be added to the excerpts for which a number has already been assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move away for the moment from the information you provided previously, Mr. Dodik, and focus a bit on some of the information you provided today. With regard to "The Islamic Declaration," in view of all the things you've said about it, was it the case or I presume it's the case that this Islamic Declaration was a hot topic at the Bosnian Serb Assembly and must have been raised repeatedly by the delegates. Is that accurate? Do you recall the extent to which "The Islamic Declaration" was addressed by members of the Bosnian Serb Assembly or the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: We were not some lunatics who were just addressing the declaration. It's a fact that it was written and so we were free to examine it. We adopted some constitutive acts there and we dealt with issues relating to the constitution. We had in mind what was Alija Izetbegovic's policy in "The Islamic Declaration" which I, myself, read several times, which promotes the things it does promote. And I think that any man who was involved in any degree in politics at the time was aware of the contents of this declaration, not only among the Serbs but among other peoples as well. And it was nothing secret. It was a published document. And when Alija Izetbegovic came to the top of his party, became its leader, it became more popular than ever among his supporters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... first seek to clarify the question. Did you mean whether the matter was addressed in assembly sessions, Mr. Tieger? Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is a timely intervention, Mr. President. Let me clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and could you please focus your answer very much on the question that's put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, I'm asking you how often, if at all, "The Islamic Declaration" was specifically raised by members of the assembly in assembly meetings. Every session, every other session, every fourth session, once in a blue moon? How -- what's the answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It was never on the agenda of our assembly as an official item on the agenda, but often various MPs referred to the contents of "The Islamic Declaration" when they explained various positions. So if I may say so now it was quite frequently, of course. But we never had an item on the agenda that would be called Islamic Declaration. Never. At least as far as I remember. Perhaps if I was absent it may have figured on the agenda. Otherwise not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we searched through every available transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm afraid that there may be some misunderstanding. Witness, you were asked how often "The Islamic Declaration" was addressed in the assembly meetings. Your answer was: "Often various MPs referred to the contents of 'The Islamic Declaration' when they explained their various positions." Now, did they refer to the content without saying this is to be found in "The Islamic Declaration," or did they refer to the content of "The Islamic Declaration" by mentioning that it was to be found in "The Islamic Declaration." You can implicitly refer to, you can explicitly refer to it as being found in "The Islamic Declaration." Could you tell us when you said they often referred to it, were those explicit references to "The Islamic Declaration" or implicit references.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most frequently it was discussed as written and stated in Alija Izetbegovic's "The Islamic Declaration", et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Specifically mentioning that document ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm talking about people who participated in the discussion and who, when explaining their positions, talked about various dangers and then they would say that such-and-such a thing was written in Alija Izetbegovic's "The Islamic Declaration." That's what I heard quite often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clarified now. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dodik, we searched through the transcripts of the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions, beginning with the first, and going on though all those in our possession which are basically the chronological versions, and we found that the first reference to "The Islamic Declaration" explicitly did not occur until the 35th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on the 2nd of October, 1993, and that -- that's found at 65 ter 02384, at e-court page 93 and B/C/S -- or Serbian page 69. And that was -- waiting for the English to come up. And for your benefit, Mr. Dodik, that can be found at the bottom third part of Mr. Goljanin's discussion where he said: "Mr. President" -- that's the third line from the bottom in English. "Mr. President, I was to remind you of the declaration that was in circulation three to four years ago. On one occasion at a session of our earlier assembly, I even spoke about that declaration. It was "The Islamic Declaration" about proclaiming an Islamic republic of BiH. There were plans there, and Sokolac, Nevesinje, et cetera, were clearly mentioned in the context of inhabiting Muslims. Okay, those were some vague formulations, which were being spread by someone, maybe even by the yellow press. But I'm getting an impression that their goal started slowly to be accomplished by those concessions that were made last time, because almost one-third of free Nevesinje was given to Turks ..." Now, Mr. Dodik, in fact, you have no reason to contest that this was the first explicit reference to "The Islamic Declaration" in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, not until October 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I have reasons to contest it. This declaration was mentioned very often in our discussions in the discussions in the assembly as well in the way that I described. Sometimes the synonym "Alija's policy" was used but we were well aware of what the "The Islamic Declaration" was and what it meant. But in terms of the form, I don't remember this particular transcript or this particular speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd tender that excerpt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They will be added to the -- no, no, this is a different transcript, yes. I'm -- I apologise. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number reserved will be P7758, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many pages do we have here, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's two in English, I believe and one in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's all, then admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, the reason - and I'm putting this to you - that "The Islamic Declaration" didn't find its way into the Bosnian Serb Assembly session discussions until then, was because, setting aside for the moment the -- whatever views were attributed to Izetbegovic on the basis of something he wrote back in the 1970s, it was widely known that Bosnian Muslims were highly Europeanised and not particularly religious, much less radical fundamentalists. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It's possible that you see it that way, but how come that so many people rallied around Alija Izetbegovic knowing what he stands for and what he had written? I am tempted to conclude that you, so many years later, you are trying to justify Alija Izetbegovic and his writing of "The Islamic Declaration." I'm not saying that all Muslims were radical but the policies that were promoted by Alija Izetbegovic were supported by almost all Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they knew that Alija Izetbegovic had served a long sentence for his religious views, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me look at a couple of contemporaneous statements from that time, not from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to 65 ter 07499, page 9 of the English, page 3 of the Serbian. And perhaps we could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're welcome to see the first page, if you want, but I can tell you, Mr. Dodik, that this is an interview with Dr. Karadzic conducted in 1990. The portion I'm going to direct your attention to is found at the very top of the middle column in Serbian, and in the middle of the page, page 9, in English, where Dr. Karadzic says: "The Islamic fundamentalism arrives to Europe with people of other race and language that makes the Europe panic. Here, the Muslims are Slavs, people with our blood and language who, for the most part, opt for the European quality of life and preservation of the Islamic faith. There is no room for panic, either among the Serbs nor among the Muslims." Mr. Dodik, that's a further reflection of the widely known fact that Bosnian Muslims were, as a rule, very Europeanised people; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: You want to say that the Serbs were not; right? I did not see this interview of Radovan Karadzic. At the time I wasn't reading his interviews, so I'm not aware of it. But you said this was from 1990, right before the war, if I understood this correctly. And this reflects his political stance at that time. I can neither confirm nor deny what he said. As you know and as I said at the beginning, I was a member of a different political party which does not mean that I have a bad opinion of Muslims. I have said here that Alija Izetbegovic was a convicted religious radical and that his policy was supported by an overwhelming majority of Muslims, almost all of them, except for a very small minority which remained in a marginalised different party like mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: We lived in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you've discussed that at length during your examination-in-chief. I'm asking you about a different aspect of the broader issue you raised. And before I go on, while I am reluctant to ever respond to comments or questions by a witness, I want to explicitly reject your comment that by pointing out that Radovan Karadzic was describing the Bosnian Muslims as Europeanised, I was somehow saying that Serbs were not. Now, let's move on to page 4 of the English in this interview and B/C/S page 1. In the third column in Serbian, one sentence of the third and the third and fourth paragraph, we see a reference to Jovo Raskovic and that reference is: "There is in the first place the high reputation of Jovo Raskovic, who is in BiH equally respected by the Serb, Croats and Muslims, since he acts as a peacemaker." And this part of the interview is Dr. Karadzic speaking also. Mr. Dodik, Jovo - or Jovan - Raskovic was the founder of the SDS party in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's commonly known.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you accept Dr. Karadzic's characterisation of his reputation and the respect in which he was held in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: At that time when these parties were just founded, we were political opponents, not sympathizers. I said before I haven't read this interview, but I can't help thinking why did you seek to indict him if he are justifying now his words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're not here to put questions to Mr. Tieger. You're here to answer his questions. Could you please stick to that principle. And could you please answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard of Jovan Raskovic, but I cannot talk about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that because you don't know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know who he is. He ... acted quietly without violence. He was active, but I could see him only on TV and in the media. I've never met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see it's time for the break, Mr. President. I tender the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 07499 will be Exhibit P7759, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Dodik, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, one question came to the mind of the Judges in this Chamber. That is, as far as the interview is concerned, do we need that interview into evidence or -- because you read out, I think, all the portions you wanted to draw our attention to literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I think it does need to be in evidence, Mr. President, because when a witness simply, unequivocally adopts it, then you have the equivalent of the document. When there is something else, then I think you need the document in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then for truth of the content or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As is the case with everything we do here, sure. I don't think we've ever made that distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll further consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, meanwhile, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we turn, please, to 65 ter 11723.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, I can tell you while this is coming onto the screen that had will be an interview for YUTEL of Jovan Raskovic. And in January 1992, I believe, as it says at the top of the page, this appeared in Svijet. And the portion I wanted to direct your attention to is found in the Serbian in the third column from the left, top half of that, and is found in the English at page 2 in the middle part of the page. And, there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first enlarge the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And no doubt we need to help -- for Mr. Dodik, the bottom part of the page, third column from the left. The bottom -- that's right now go to the third column, that's it, and if you could enlarge the top half of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There, Dr. Raskovic states: "I believe that there is no fear of Bosnian sovereignty for the Serbian people in BiH. It would not be genocide. Maybe it would not be Serbophile, and it would be Srbophobe but it wouldn't be Srbocide either. I talked about that with Karadzic. He is not inclined to accept my opinion. He thinks it is necessary to react in a different way if the Bosnian sovereignty is formed. According to him, the Serbs must adopt a different political stand and a diverse political procedure in that case, even though it seems to me that it pushes people into a war." Mr. Dodik, were you aware of such differing views about the risks of sovereignty or Muslim rule generally, if it came to that, among Serbian politicians?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: To the extent I was able to understand, this is from January 1991 or 1992? When?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: 1992. Of course, I didn't see before and I don't know anything about this view of Mr. Raskovic but if it matters I don't agree with his position. I don't know what views Karadzic presented in that conversation, but if it matters, I can tell you what I think and what I thought then. I was convinced --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I really don't like to interrupt you, but you have provided an answer to the question, and I'd like to move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 11723, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7760, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Tieger, I still have some difficulties in understanding that the witness has answered the question. The question was whether he was aware of differing views on the matter. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take your point, Mr. President. I was actually trying to forestall a move into areas even farther away from my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I can imagine that you wanted the witness to come back to your question but then also, perhaps, to answer it. Were you aware of views among politicians differing in a way as described in this article between the different views of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Raskovic? I'm not specifically asking about these two but are there different views? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we turn next to 65 ter 02366 beginning at page 95 in the English and page 64 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, I had asked you earlier about the -- what I termed the well-known understanding that Bosnian Muslims were Europeanised and not particularly religious. In that connection I earlier directed you to a comment by Dr. Karadzic. Now I want to direct your attention to a comment by Mr. Krajisnik. And this is a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, I believe, held in January 1993, the 24th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and if we look at the beginning in the middle of the page in English, and similarly situated on the page in front of you in B/C/S, we see Mr. Kupresanin speaking. He says: "We stumbled over some ideas several times in the past. Gentlemen, is the Muslim nation a nation at all?" He continues talking about the -- it was created in Tito conception in 1994. "Should we deny this --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 1974. Thank you, Your Honour. "Should we deny this nation as a nation." He continues a couple of lines down: "It was since the time remembered a Serb country. It is true that Turks were here for sometime, for 500 years. We threw out the Turks, we threw out the Austrians and we threw out the Germans, and yet Bosnia isn't Serb but Muslim of the non-existent nation. Are these not Serb stupidities again?" And he then notes: "I propose that we deny the Muslims as a nation on the next session of the assembly." And then we see Mr. Krajisnik speak on the next page in the English, and still on the same page in Serbian, although it will continue and he says: "I think that Mr. Kupresanin is right, and I was wrong when I once said: Don't put them together with us. Because, if you push them together with us, we do not know what to do with them. I think this should be corrected a little. We should really take a stand concerning whether the Muslims are a nation. Here, we had one suggestion that we say they are a Muslim sect of Turkish orientation because it would then create a discord in the Muslim world. Namely, Saudi Arabia and other Muslim countries believe that the Turks are fake Muslims, who eat and drink like the others. It is known that they are not so religious." So here, too, Mr. Dodik, Mr. Krajisnik is acknowledging the well-known fact that the Bosnian Muslims were not considered particularly religious, much less radical fundamentalists; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That's Krajisnik's opinion. I was talking about Izetbegovic and his radical orientation and faith. I said there was a general perception that Bosnian Muslims were the most secular in Europe, certainly. But they still supported the policy of Alija Izetbegovic. I don't know what I'm supposed to do here. I would like to make a correction, if I may. We were not the Assembly of Bosnian Serbs. We were the Assembly of Republika Srpska, and I would appreciate it if you would use that name, which is proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in your last question, you've woven in that it's a well-known fact. Could you always please clearly distinguish between what someone says is his opinion and whether that's a well-known fact or not. These are two separate issues and I'd like -- witness may be confused by such an interwoven element in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can answer it -- ask it again but I see -- based on the answer, I don't see a confusion here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a general matter of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just continue on this point, as long as we're on this issue, with what happened at that assembly session after Mr. Krajisnik announced that he agreed with Mr. Kupresanin. He continues and says: "Here, Vojo, you were right and I wasn't." And he asks at the end of this intervention: "Does anyone have anything against that the Muslims are not a nation?" Then we hear from Mr. Corda, or the Assembly hears from Mr. Corda, and on the next page in English and I believe the next page in -- page 65 of the e-court in Serbian, Krajisnik, again, responds: "Well, all right, people, if we accept that they are some kind of a group, Turkish or I don't know whose, then we simply give them aces to their hands to be an independent nation." And then a line later, he says: "Why, we should tell them what they really are. They are unbelievers, a nation that is not a nation, that is to say, a nation that would like to be a nation but has no arguments for a nation." Savo Knezevic then speaks and he continues the discussion about four lines after he begins: "May God give that they never again be part of our nation. We don't need him who once betrayed anymore. They are Mohamedans of Turkish provenance and nothing else. They are not even the real members of Islam because they are more of a sect than real members of Islam. And a Muslim is some sort of the member of Islam. They are some kind of a lower category." And then on the next page in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in all fairness to the witness, would you allow him to read at least this paragraph, because you pick out just a sentence here, a sentence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think it is fair to the witness that he has an opportunity to read what Mr. Knezevic said, and I think -- are we still on the right page, 4. If we go back, then we could also read the whole of the ... Witness, once you've read the portion of which elements were read out to you by Mr. Tieger, please let us know. Well, Witness, you are given an opportunity to read the whole of what Mr. Knezevic said, but then you would have to look at your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll now turn to what Mr. Krajisnik says to conclude it. At the bottom of page 97 in English and on page 66 of the Serbian. "Shall we then now take the Muslims out of Serbism forever? All right, gentlemen, can we now make up our mind and take a position that the Muslims as a nation are the Communistic creation. We do not accept this artificial nation. We believe that the Muslims are a sect, a group or a party of Turkish provenance. "Does anyone have anything else to add? No? I put these conclusions to a vote. Who is for" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Is there anyone against, abstaining? Gentlemen, thank you, we adopted the conclusions unanimously."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I wanted to put Mr. Krajisnik's comments about the relative religious nature of the Muslim community in context and we see the full context, I believe, from what I've just read out. I wanted to ask you, Mr. Dodik, were you among the assembly delegates at that session who voted for the proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I believe you have that information. I myself don't remember. Where was this session held? You probably have it noted somewhere who attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document itself says, I think it's in Bijeljina on page 2 if -- if it's the 24th Session, then the document states on page 2 that it was held on the 8th, 1993 in Bijeljina. That must be a small mistake. But on the cover page, it says the 8th of January of 1993, Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, but there is a record. Records of attendance. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender that excerpt and ask that it be added to any that exists for that session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need -- let me just check. You have already made an excerpt, and we add it to any that exist. Does there exist any? There does. And then this can be added to the excerpt already in the system. Under what number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This may be added to P6921 and it has been uploaded already. No, it has not uploaded already. It will be uploaded. And Mr. Registrar is hereby instructed to add it to the excerpts already known under P6921. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, during the course of your examination-in-chief, there was considerable emphasis on not only "The Islamic Declaration" but on general activities by Mr. Izetbegovic or the SDA or the Muslims generally. And in -- in -- in respect of actions taken or not taken by the Bosnian Serbs, I wanted to put this to you and that is that Mr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership for quite some time, and certainly beginning in 1991, knew what they wanted to do but simply waited for a -- some form of pretext to act and that steps taken or that actions taken following anything done by the Muslim side reflected pre-planned steps to be implemented at opportune moments. That's the reality of the developments in 1991 through 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That's your hypothesis which underlies your entire work. They did not tell me what they intended, and I did not have the impression that what was done by the Serbs was action. It was, rather, reaction. I don't think you are right when you say it was pre-planned. I don't know about any such plan. I never saw it, and I didn't hear about it even later. All I know is that when we discussed these objectives that the assembly adopted in 1992, there was a lot of pressure for this topic to be discussed which, in my view, denies the existence of any pre-planning. I didn't know about any plans at the time, and since then, I haven't seen any evidence that it existed. It was reaction to the developments. And you can see, if you look at it chronologically, which events preceded other events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab -- the tab to 65 ter 07704. Mr. Dodik, what will come up on the screen is a transcript from a SFRY Presidency meeting held in December of 1991. And I'd like to turn to page 78 of the English and page 105 of the Serbian. The portion I'll direct your attention is found at approximately the fourth sentence from the top and, in English, in the middle of the page. And there, Dr. Karadzic is speaking and is explaining to the members of the SFRY Presidency the following: "We have made a list of moves. Ten moves in the direction we want, so that there are results. Bosnia remains in Yugoslavia, either as a whole or our areas. But we won't do anything until Alija messes something up. When Alija messes something up, we make move number 5 and then we wait. When Alija messes something else up - we make move number 6." So, Mr. Dodik, I know you indicated earlier that Mr. Karadzic wasn't necessarily telling you his plans, but here we see a reflection of what he was telling others at the time about what he had planned and how he intended to implement it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I did not attend that Presidency session. I'm not aware of this. I had no chance to familiarize myself with this, and it turns out that Alija really messed things up many times, as there was so much need to emphasise this. I mean, I cannot either deny this or confirm it. Obviously, if it was said at the Presidency session, then it was. I am not aware of any plan that had been prepared beforehand. I didn't know about it and I think it's more hypothetical. If he messes things up, we do thing number 5; if he does it again, we do thing number 6. I think it's more a hypothesis than a serious plan. But I cannot really either confirm or deny it, I can only say once again that I'm not aware of any precise or specific plan that existed previously in the period that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's 2.15, Mr. President. I tender that and I think it's time to end the session.
